title: Winter Swans

facts.type: Six tercets (3-line stanzas) and a final couplet; no regular rhyme
facts.exam: Yes: printed in June 2019; also a suggested partner in the 2017, 2018, Nov 2021, 2022 and 2024 mark schemes
facts.partner: Porphyria's Lover (your anchor); Love's Philosophy also works well

themes.name: Commitment
themes.src: AQA mark scheme 2019 (“enduring / lasting romantic relationships”); 2018 (“more established relationships”)

themes.name: Nature
themes.src: AQA mark schemes 2024 (“nature in ‘Winter Swans’”) and 2022 (“nature imagery in … ‘Winter Swans’”)

cards.story: After what seems to have been a quarrel, a couple walk silently round a lake in winter. Swans on the lake make them stop. By the end, without a word, they are holding hands again.
cards.message: Love can heal itself after a quarrel. Sometimes the healing happens through actions and touch, not through talking.
cards.why: Sheers's collection Skirrid Hill is named after a Welsh hill whose name comes from a word meaning “divorce or separation”. Most of its love poems end in parting; this is one where the couple come back together. Swansea University CREW; Seren

title_note.heading: The title
title_note.text: Winter is the cold, dead season: a picture of a relationship at a low point. Swans are famous for staying with one partner: Britannica says plainly, “They mate for life.” So the title puts a bleak time and a symbol of lasting love side by side, and the poem moves from the first to the second.
title_note.src: Britannica (swans); the link to the relationship is our reading

synopsis.setup: The speaker (“I”) remembers a walk with a partner (“you”) after two days of rain. We are never told what has gone wrong between them, only that they are “silent and apart”.

steps.text: The rain has finally stopped. The clouds have “given their all”, and in the break the couple go for a walk.
The ground is soaked and seems to gulp for air at their feet. They walk round the edge of the lake without speaking, keeping their distance.
Swans appear and stop them. The swans tip forwards together, in perfect time, as if heavy weights were rolling down to their heads.
Half of each swan disappears under the dark water, leaving white feathers showing like icebergs. Then they pop back up, like boats righting themselves in a storm.
The partner breaks the silence: “They mate for life”. The swans glide away, white as china. The speaker doesn't answer, and the couple walk on into the afternoon light.
Walking slowly over the stones and sand, the speaker notices that their hands have somehow found each other. They are folded together like a pair of wings settling after flight.

synopsis.turn: The turning point (lines 13–14): the partner's words “They mate for life” and the speaker's silence. Nobody says sorry, but straight afterwards the couple start to come back together.
synopsis.ending: On the joined hands, not on words. The final image is calm and settled: the storm in the relationship has passed, like the rain at the start.
synopsis.tone: Quiet, tense and awkward at first; gentle, hopeful and tender by the end.

poem_intro: Highlighted words are the ones worth quoting in the exam.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>The clouds had given their all</mark> … <mark>then a break</mark>
poem_blocks.note: The rain has stopped after two days, as if the clouds are exhausted. A “break” is a gap in the weather, and also a pause in an argument. The couple walk in it.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>gulping for breath at our feet</mark> … <mark>silent and apart,</mark>
poem_blocks.note: The soaked ground is personified: it gasps for air like someone drowning or crying. The couple “skirted” the lake (went round the edge), not speaking and not touching. Skirting can also mean avoiding a problem.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>until the swans came and stopped us</mark> … <mark>tipping in unison.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: The swans interrupt them. “In unison” means perfectly together: the opposite of the couple. The swans move as if “rolling weights” down their bodies, a heavy image that may hint at the couple's burden.

With their heads underwater, only half of each swan shows. “Icebergs” suggests coldness and hidden depths. Then they come up again “like boats righting in rough weather”: they recover from the storm, as the couple will.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>'They mate for life' you said</mark> … <mark>porcelain over the stilling water.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: The only words spoken in the poem. The swans glide away, white and smooth as porcelain (fine china), which is beautiful but breakable. The water is “stilling” (calming). The speaker doesn't reply.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>I noticed our hands</mark> … <mark>swum the distance between us</mark> … <mark>like a pair of wings settling after flight.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: On the stony shore, the speaker realises their hands have joined without either of them deciding. “Swum” links the couple to the swans. The final simile shows them as one pair, calm again.

quotes.q: The clouds had given their all
quotes.means: the rain has finally run out.
quotes.why: the clouds are personified as if they have argued themselves out; the storm may stand for the couple's quarrel.
quotes.tech: personification; pathetic fallacy (weather that matches feelings)

quotes.q: gulping for breath at our feet
quotes.means: the soaked ground seems to gasp for air.
quotes.why: the relationship is drowning too; AQA's 2019 mark scheme picks out “gulping” as a word worth analysing.

quotes.means: they don't speak and don't touch.
quotes.why: sums up the couple's distance in three words; the rest of the poem undoes both.
quotes.tech: pair of adjectives; caesura (the comma before it slows the line)

quotes.q: As if rolling weights down their bodies
quotes.means: the swans tip forward heavily as they feed.
quotes.why: the heaviness may suggest the weight of the couple's problems; AQA's 2019 mark scheme names “weights”.

quotes.means: swans stay with one partner until death.
quotes.why: the only speech in the poem: perhaps an indirect way of asking whether the couple will last too.

quotes.means: the swans glide away, white and smooth, as the water calms.
quotes.why: porcelain is precious but fragile, like love; “stilling” shows the storm calming. AQA's 2019 mark scheme names “porcelain”.

quotes.means: their hands have moved together without them noticing.
quotes.why: the hands act on their own, as if their bodies make peace before their minds do; “swum” links them to the swans.

quotes.q: like a pair of wings settling after flight
quotes.means: their joined hands are calm and together, like a resting bird's wings.
quotes.why: the couple become one “pair”, like the swans; “settling” shows the conflict is over.

form.heading: The form: three-line stanzas that settle into a pair
explain: A tercet is “a unit or group of three lines of verse, usually containing rhyme.” Britannica
A couplet is “two successive lines of poetry, often rhymed”: a stanza that is “a couple, a pairing”. poets.org

Sheers's poems in Skirrid Hill usually have no regular metre or rhyme scheme. Most have at least one full rhyme, “frequently supplemented by internal rhymes, assonance, and half rhymes.” Swansea University CREW; Poetry Archive
Half rhyme: words that nearly rhyme, such as “water” and “weather”. Enjambment: when a sentence runs on past the end of a line or stanza without a pause.
this_poem: 20 lines: six tercets, then a final two-line couplet. our count
Three becomes two: the uneven three-line stanzas suit a couple who are out of step. The poem ends in a couplet, a “pairing”, just as the couple become a pair again. our reading

Sentences flow across stanzas (for example lines 6–7 and 18–19). The long, run-on sentences feel like a slow walk, and the last sentence carries the hands across the stanza break until they “folded”. our reading

Sound echoes, not a rhyme scheme: “water” (line 10) half-rhymes with “weather” (line 12), and “light” (line 15) fully rhymes with the poem's last word, “flight”. The couplet itself doesn't rhyme (“other” / “flight”), so the ending is gentle rather than neat. our check
First person, past tense: the speaker looks back. A Sheers resource warns that first person heightens emotion, but “we must be wary of a simplistically biographical reading.” Swansea University CREW
form.say: A sentence you could use: Sheers writes in uneven three-line stanzas while the couple are “silent and apart”, but ends with a couplet, a pair of lines for a couple who have become a pair again, so the form itself shows the relationship coming back together.

methods.title: Weather that matches the feelings
methods.text: The poem begins after a storm: <q>“The clouds had given their all”</q>. The ground is <q>“gulping for breath”</q>. By the end the couple walk in <q>“afternoon light”</q>. The weather clears as the relationship does.
methods.def: when the weather or setting reflects people's feelings.

methods.title: The swans as a symbol
methods.text: The swans move <q>“in unison”</q> while the couple are apart. <q>“They mate for life”</q> turns them into a model of lasting love. The hands become <q>“a pair of wings”</q>, so the couple end up like the swans.
methods.def: an object that stands for a bigger idea.

methods.title: Actions, not words
methods.text: Only one sentence is spoken, and the speaker <q>“didn't reply”</q>. Instead the hands <q>“swum the distance between us”</q>, as if their bodies make up before their minds do. AQA's 2019 mark scheme points to “the use of hands, or swans, or the natural world”.
methods.def: giving human actions or feelings to something that is not human.

methods.title: Surprising comparisons
methods.text: Swans are <q>“icebergs of white feather”</q>, <q>“boats righting in rough weather”</q> and <q>“porcelain”</q>. Each image mixes strength and danger or fragility: love can survive storms, but it can also break.
methods.def: describing one thing as if it were another (metaphor), or saying it is “like” another (simile).

warn: Examiners warn: don't just describe the stanza shape. AQA's 2022 report says “There is a risk of comments on poetic construction becoming rather descriptive”. Always say what the form shows about the relationship.

items.text: Born in Suva, the capital of Fiji, in 1974. He moved to London aged three and to Abergavenny, in Wales, aged nine.
items.src: Swansea University CREW; Poetry Archive; Wales Literature Exchange

items.text: He sees himself as Welsh: “for as long as I can remember … I’ve identified as Welsh.”
He says landscape came first: “I fell in love with landscape before I fell in love with poetry”. This helps explain why nature does so much work in his love poems.
A prize-winning writer of poems, novels and plays: an Eric Gregory Award, the Somerset Maugham Award, and Wales Book of the Year twice. He is now a professor at Swansea University.
items.src: Poetry Archive; Wales Literature Exchange; Seren

cards.title: The book it comes from: Skirrid Hill (2005)

items.text: Winter Swans is in Skirrid Hill, published by Seren in 2005. It won the Somerset Maugham Award in 2006.
items.src: Swansea University CREW; Poetry Archive; Seren

items.text: The title is a hill near Abergavenny. Its name comes from Welsh words meaning “divorce or separation”, which is one of the book's main themes.
In the book, relationships are “almost invariably” broken “by death, disagreement, or some other parting”. Winter Swans stands out because the couple come back together.
items.care: one source; the contrast with Winter Swans is our reading

items.text: A Swansea University teaching resource picks out Winter Swans for a recurring image: “lovers fitting together perfectly”, like the hands that fold “like a pair of wings settling after flight”.
Local legend says the hill split at the moment of Christ's crucifixion: a parting that also holds the idea of return and “a transformed relationship”.

cards.title: Swans: the facts behind the symbol

items.text: General knowledge: swans really do pair for life. Britannica: “They mate for life.”
Swan “divorce” is rare: one study puts it as low as 3%. Interesting next to a book named after a word for divorce.
items.care: one source; the link is our reading

items.text: Swans feed by dipping their heads and “sometimes tipping forwards so that only their tail feathers poke up”. This is the real behaviour behind <q>“tipping in unison”</q>.
Pairs perform a “synchronised courtship display” on the water, which can form “a heart shape”.
His rhymes are irregular, often half rhymes and internal rhymes rather than a fixed pattern.
He brings together words “from very different areas to create unusual and startling images”, like icebergs, boats and porcelain for swans.
His love poems focus on “touch as well as sight”. Another poem in the book says “bodies, like souls,/ only exist when touched.”
He credits the Welsh poet R. S. Thomas with having “introduced me to the beauty of economy” (saying a lot in few words).

context.ao3: Putting it into an answer (AO3): Winter Swans comes from Skirrid Hill (2005), a collection named after a hill whose Welsh name comes from a word meaning “divorce or separation”, in which most relationships end in parting. Against that background, Sheers's couple, who begin “silent and apart” but end like “a pair of wings”, offer rare hope: love that has been through a storm can last, as swans' does.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: June 2019 mark scheme (Winter Swans question): “romantic feelings, either positive or negative, such as compared with … ‘Porphyria’s Lover’” and “person/direct address”
similar: Both open with bad weather that matches the mood: Sheers's walk comes just after <q>“two days of rain”</q>, and Browning begins with <q>“The rain set early in to-night,”</q> with a <q>“sullen wind”</q>.
Both lovers fail to speak at a key moment: Sheers's speaker <q>“didn't reply”</q>; Porphyria's lover stays silent too: <q>“When no voice replied,”</q>
Both end with a couple sitting or moving together, close and still: <q>“folded, one over the other,”</q> and <q>“And thus we sit together now,”</q>
different: Healing vs destroying: Sheers's silence leads to touch and peace. Browning's leads to murder: “And strangled her.”
Two people vs one: in Winter Swans the hands join by themselves, as equals. Browning's speaker wants to own her: “That moment she was mine, mine, fair,”
Who speaks: in Winter Swans the partner gets the only spoken words. In Porphyria's Lover she never speaks directly; we only hear him, so we cannot trust what he says.
Ending: Sheers ends in calm hope (“settling after flight”); Browning ends in an unsettling silence: “And yet God has not said a word!”

comparisons.aqa: AQA: June 2024 mark scheme (Neutral Tones question) suggests Winter Swans first, for “bleak and more positive views of love” and “hope for the future in ‘Winter Swans’”
similar: Almost the same scene: a couple by water in winter. <q>“We stood by a pond that winter day,”</q> and <q>“as we skirted the lake, silent and apart,”</q>
Both speak to the partner as “you” and use nature to show the state of the relationship.
different: The relationship that heals vs the one that dies: Sheers's couple come back together; Hardy's love is already dead: “The smile on your mouth was the deadest thing”
Nature: Sheers's swans bring the couple together. Hardy's grey leaves and white sun only show what is lost: “And a pond edged with greyish leaves.”
Ending: Sheers ends on a new image of togetherness. Hardy's poem circles back to the same pond, as if he is trapped in the memory.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: June 2019 mark scheme: “the hope in ‘Winter Swans’ with the less hopeful … ‘Love’s Philosophy’” and the contrast between the start and end of “‘Winter Swans’ with ‘Love’s Philosophy’”
similar: Both use pairs in nature to argue that people belong together: swans that <q>“mate for life”</q>, and rivers and waves that join: <q>“Nothing in the world is single;”</q>
Both use an image of two becoming one: <q>“a pair of wings”</q> and <q>“In one another's being mingle —”</q>
different: Words vs silence: Shelley's speaker argues hard, with questions and commands. Sheers's speaker says nothing; the reunion just happens.
Ending: Love's Philosophy ends unanswered: “If thou kiss not me?” Winter Swans ends with the couple already together: more hopeful.
Stage of love: Shelley's speaker wants a love that hasn't started; Sheers's couple are repairing one that already exists.

exam_box.question: Compare how poets present romantic feelings in ‘Winter Swans’ and in one other poem from ‘Love and relationships’. (AQA, June 2019)
exam_box.thesis: Both poets show romantic feelings tested by silence and storms, but Sheers shows love quietly healing, while Browning shows a lover's need to possess turning into violence.
exam_box.para: Both poets use stormy weather to show romantic feelings under strain. Sheers's couple walk after <q>“two days of rain”</q>, <q>“silent and apart”</q>, as if the storm was their argument. Browning's speaker also waits through a storm, listening <q>“with heart fit to break.”</q> In both poems a lover stays silent at the key moment: Sheers's speaker <q>“didn't reply”</q>, and Porphyria's lover answers with <q>“no voice”</q>. However, the silences lead to opposite places. Sheers's hands <q>“swum the distance between us”</q>, a gentle personification that shows love mending itself without words. Browning's speaker instead wants to own her, <q>“mine, mine”</q>, and kills her. Where Sheers ends with the couple as <q>“a pair of wings”</q>, equal and settled, Browning ends with one living person and a corpse.
why: Opens with a clear point about romantic feelings, the exact focus of the question
Short quotations from both poems, with methods named (weather, silence, personification)
Compares all the way through (“also”, “However”, “Where…”) and ends on a judgement
